title: How Triage Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain triage, the system of sorting patients by urgency of need. They trace its origin to Napoleon's chief surgeon Dominique Jean Larrey, who devised battlefield sorting in the 1790s, and cover later refinements by British naval surgeon John Wilson in the 1840s and the shift toward treating those most likely to return to battle in World War One. They describe modern emergency room triage, including the Manchester Triage System and color codes (which differ between countries and hospitals), the Met Tag invented by Robert Blodgett in Jacksonville, Florida after the Cuban missile crisis and later revised by Dennis Ortiz and his brother of LA County Fire Department, and field triage scoring. They close with criticism of triage, a study finding longer waits for the most urgent patients, and a Kaiser Permanente lean approach that treated minor injuries in the waiting room. The episode ends with listener mail about lighthouses, including Terrible Tilly.

entities.name: Kaiser Permanente South Sacramento Medical Center

segments.title: Opening banter and French origin of 'triage'
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Scotland shirts and their UK tour, then discuss the French word 'trier' meaning to sort, especially for vegetables, as the origin of the term triage.

segments.title: Larrey and the origins of battlefield triage
segments.summary: Napoleon's chief surgeon Dominique Jean Larrey devised a system to prioritize wounded soldiers by severity of injury, replacing earlier treatment by social standing. Napoleon reportedly still expected to be at the top. John Wilson in the 1840s shifted focus to those likely to survive, and in World War One the emphasis moved to treating people who could quickly return to battle.

segments.title: Triage at the emergency room
segments.summary: Hosts describe the ER triage nurse, a host's personal Beth Israel visit, and the Manchester Triage System flow chart that focuses heavily on breathing. Triage includes vitals and medical history, and there are two tracks for less severe cases.

segments.title: ER color codes
segments.summary: Hosts explain that triage color codes are not universal. In the US, code blue is most urgent and code red is serious, with orange, gray, and green following. Under the Manchester scale, red is worst and blue is less urgent. Hosts argue for a universal system.

segments.title: Incident triage intro
segments.summary: Brief note that triage applies whenever resources are scarce and demand is high, including mass-casualty incidents such as explosions.

segments.title: Met Tag invented by Robert Blodgett
segments.summary: Robert Blodgett, civil defense director in Jacksonville, Florida, created a two-sided lanyard tag with color codes during the Cuban missile crisis. Tags were torn off to show progressively worse condition, ending with a black morgue tag. After the Oklahoma City bombing, Dennis Ortiz and his brother of LA County Fire Department revised the tag for terrorist disasters.

segments.title: Field triage score and spectrum of triage
segments.summary: Triage exists on a spectrum from calm ER to mass disaster. Battlefield field triage score combines pulse and Glasgow Coma Scale awareness to predict survival. Status can change, so tags may be updated.

segments.title: Criticism of triage and Kaiser Permanente approach
segments.summary: Hosts discuss complaints about ER wait times and people leaving without being seen. A 1990s study found triage led to longer waits for the most critical patients without improving satisfaction. Kaiser Permanente South Sacramento used lean principles to treat minor injuries in the waiting room, cutting left-without-being-seen rates and wait times.

segments.title: Lighthouse follow-up listener mail
segments.summary: A listener named Kendra writes about lighthouses on Oregon's coast, highlighting Terrible Tilly, an offshore lighthouse built on a rock where sailors' ashes were stored.
